item.title: Cloud Native Architect Learning Path
item.description: About three weeks at one to two hours a day covers the whole path. Short on time? Read the two case studies, then the quick check, and fill gaps from the linked articles.

item.title: Containers, Images and Docker
item.description:
Simple definition#

A container is a normal Linux process that the kernel isolates — it gets its own view of files, network and processes, and limited CPU and memory. A container image is a portable package of the application and everything it needs (runtime, libraries, config defaults), built in layers and stored in a registry.

item.title: Kubernetes Architecture: Control Plane, Nodes and Reconciliation
item.description:
Simple definition#

Kubernetes is an open-source platform that runs containerised applications across a cluster of machines. You tell it what you want — “run three copies of this image, reachable on port 8080” — and it continuously works to make the cluster match, restarting, rescheduling and replacing containers as machines and workloads change.

item.title: Platform Engineering Fundamentals
item.description:
Simple definition#

Platform engineering is the discipline of building and running internal platforms — curated, self-service capabilities for infrastructure, delivery, security and operations — so that application teams can deliver software quickly and safely without each team becoming an expert in Kubernetes, cloud, networking and compliance.

item.title: Quick Check: Cloud Native & Platform Engineering
item.description:
Answers are short — enough to check your understanding. Each section links to the articles with full explanations.

TipHow to use this page

Cover the answer, explain it in your own words, then compare. Mark anything you hesitated on and reread the linked article. Aim for 80% before moving on.

item.title: SRE Fundamentals: SLOs, Error Budgets and Incident Management
item.description:
Simple definition#

Site reliability engineering (SRE) applies software engineering to operations. Its central idea: decide how reliable a service needs to be (a Service Level Objective), measure it, and use the gap between 100% and the objective — the error budget — to balance reliability work against feature delivery.

item.title: Internal Developer Platforms: Architecture and Tools
item.description:
Simple definition#

An internal developer platform (IDP) is the sum of tools, APIs, templates and automation that a platform team integrates into self-service golden paths. A developer portal (such as Backstage) is the front door to the IDP — but the portal is not the platform; the automation behind it is.

item.title: Running Kubernetes in Practice
item.description:
Simple definition#

“Running Kubernetes” covers day 1 (creating clusters and deploying apps) and day 2 (upgrading, scaling, securing, backing up and operating them for years). Most of the cost and risk of Kubernetes is in day 2.

item.title: Observability with OpenTelemetry
item.description:
Simple definition#

Monitoring tells you whether known things are wrong (dashboards and alerts on predefined metrics). Observability lets you ask why — including questions you did not anticipate — by exploring rich, correlated telemetry: metrics, logs, traces and increasingly profiles.

item.title: Platform Review Checklist
item.description:
How to use it#

Use this checklist to review your own design before building, or a team’s design at an architecture board or production-readiness review. Score each area 0–3 and record evidence.

1. Goals and SLOs#

  • Business goals and users defined? SLOs, RTO and RPO per service tier?
  • Red flags: “five nines” for everything; no owner per service.

2. Cluster topology#

  • Managed or self-managed — and why? How many clusters, by environment/region/tenancy? Zones?
  • Upgrade cadence and process? Clusters reproducible from code?
  • Red flags: hand-built snowflake clusters; versions more than two minors behind; single-zone production.

3. Workloads#

  • Requests/limits, probes, PDBs, topology spread, autoscaling for every production workload?
  • Stateful services on managed databases or mature operators? Backups tested?
  • Red flags: BestEffort Pods in prod; liveness probes that check dependencies; databases without tested restore.

4. Networking#

  • Gateway API (not ingress-nginx); TLS everywhere; DNS automation?
  • Default-deny NetworkPolicies; egress control; IP plan for growth?
  • Service mesh justified?
  • Red flags: one LoadBalancer per app; flat network; retired ingress controller.

5. Security#

  • OIDC for humans; least-privilege RBAC; no cluster-admin for CI or apps?
  • Pod Security restricted; policy as code enforced; secrets in an external store; workload identity?
  • Signed images verified at admission; SBOMs; runtime detection; audit logs?
  • Red flags: secrets in Git; :latest images; privileged Pods; shared admin kubeconfigs.

6. Delivery#

  • Build once, promote by digest; DevSecOps scans; GitOps pull model?
  • Progressive delivery with automated analysis and rollback? Database migration strategy?
  • Change management automated with evidence; release orchestration where needed?
  • Red flags: CI with production credentials; manual helm upgrade in prod; per-environment rebuilds.

7. Platform and developer experience#

  • Golden paths for common tasks; catalog with owners; self-service infrastructure APIs?
  • Platform run as a product with users, roadmap, metrics and SLOs?
  • Red flags: ticket-driven provisioning; portal without automation; mandated tools nobody likes.

8. Observability and resilience#

  • OpenTelemetry instrumentation; metrics, logs, traces correlated; SLO burn-rate alerts; runbooks?
  • Timeouts, retries (one layer), circuit breakers; DR strategy per tier; drills; chaos experiments?
  • Red flags: alerts on CPU only; no tracing; untested DR.

9. Cost and operations#

  • Cost allocation by team (labels enforced); showback; budgets and anomaly alerts?
  • Rightsizing, autoscaling, spot, commitments, non-prod schedules?
  • On-call, incident process, postmortems, platform team capacity?
  • Red flags: no cost visibility; requests far above usage; heroic on-call.

Scoring rubric#

Score Meaning
0 Missing
1 Mentioned, not designed
2 Designed with some gaps
3 Designed and evidenced (tests, numbers, prototypes, drills)

Ready for production when no area is 0, security and resilience score 3 for Tier 0/1 services, and all gaps have owners and dates.

item.title: Workloads, Scheduling, Autoscaling and Storage
item.description:
Simple definition#

A workload is an application running on Kubernetes. The smallest unit is a Pod — one or more containers that share a network identity and storage. You rarely create Pods directly; you use controllers (Deployment, StatefulSet, DaemonSet, Job) that create and manage Pods for you.

item.title: Developer Experience: Measuring and Improving It
item.description:
Simple definition#

Developer experience (DevEx) is how developers feel about, think about and value their work environment — tools, processes, platforms and culture. Good DevEx lets developers spend their time on valuable work instead of waiting, searching and fighting friction. It is the main outcome a platform team should improve.

item.title: Kubernetes Networking: Pods, Services, Gateway API and Network Policy
item.description:
Simple definition#

Kubernetes networking answers four questions: how Pods talk to each other, how clients find a stable address for a changing set of Pods (Services), how external traffic gets in (Gateway API / Ingress), and how traffic is restricted (NetworkPolicy).

item.title: Red Hat OpenShift
item.description:
Simple definition#

Red Hat OpenShift is an enterprise Kubernetes platform: certified Kubernetes plus an integrated, supported set of components — operating system, networking, ingress, registry, monitoring, logging, security, CI/CD, GitOps, service mesh, virtualization and a developer portal — installed and upgraded as one product.

item.title: Cloud Native Quick Reference
item.description:
Kubernetes objects at a glance#

Need Object
Stateless app Deployment (+ HPA, PDB)
Stateful app StatefulSet + PVC (or operator / managed service)
Per-node agent DaemonSet
Batch / scheduled Job / CronJob
Stable address Service
North-south traffic Gateway + HTTPRoute
Config / secrets ConfigMap / Secret (+ External Secrets)
Isolation & budgets Namespace, ResourceQuota, LimitRange, NetworkPolicy
Availability during drains PodDisruptionBudget
New API types CRD + operator

kubectl essentials#

kubectl get pods -n shop -o wide            # what is running where
kubectl describe pod <pod> -n shop          # events and reasons
kubectl logs deploy/orders -n shop -f       # logs
kubectl events -n shop --types=Warning      # recent problems
kubectl diff -f k8s/                        # preview changes
kubectl rollout status deploy/orders        # watch a rollout
kubectl rollout undo deploy/orders          # roll back
kubectl debug -it <pod> --image=busybox     # ephemeral debug container
kubectl auth can-i delete pods --as=jane    # check RBAC
kubectl top pods -n shop                    # resource usage

Secure defaults#

Area Default
Pod security Namespace label pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce: restricted
Container non-root, read-only root FS, drop ALL capabilities, seccomp RuntimeDefault
Network Default-deny NetworkPolicy + explicit allows (incl. DNS)
Images Minimal base, scanned, signed, SBOM, deployed by digest
Secrets External store + External Secrets Operator; etcd encryption at rest
Access OIDC humans, least-privilege RBAC, read-only prod, workload identity for Pods

Delivery#

Topic Rule of thumb
Artifacts Build once, sign, promote by digest
Packaging Helm for packages, Kustomize for overlays
Deployment GitOps pull (Argo CD / Flux); folders per environment, not branches
Rollout Canary with automated analysis (Argo Rollouts / Flagger)
Secrets in Git Never plaintext: External Secrets, Sealed Secrets or SOPS
Governance Risk-based automated approvals; orchestration for multi-team releases
DORA Deploy frequency, lead time, change failure rate, recovery time

Platform engineering#

Concept One-liner
Platform as a product Developers are customers; adoption is earned
Golden path Opinionated supported route with guardrails
IDP planes Developer control, integration & delivery, resources, observability, security
Portal Backstage: catalog, templates, TechDocs, plugins
Infra APIs Crossplane / kro claims and compositions
DevEx Feedback loops, cognitive load, flow state
Maturity aspects Investment, adoption, interfaces, operations, measurement

SLO maths#

SLO Downtime / 30 days Error budget
99% 7.2 h 1%
99.5% 3.6 h 0.5%
99.9% 43 min 0.1%
99.95% 22 min 0.05%
99.99% 4.3 min 0.01%

Fast-burn page (99.9% SLO): burn rate ≥ 14.4 over 1 h and 5 min = 2% of monthly budget in one hour.

item.title: Resilience Engineering and Disaster Recovery
item.description:
Simple definition#

Resilience is a system’s ability to keep serving users — perhaps in a degraded way — when parts fail, and to recover quickly. Disaster recovery (DR) is the plan and capability to restore service and data after a large failure such as losing a region.

item.title: System Design: An Internal Developer Platform for 300 Teams
item.description:
The design brief#

“A bank with 300 delivery teams (about 2,500 developers) runs a mix of VMs and early Kubernetes clusters. New services take six weeks to reach production through tickets. Design an internal developer platform that gets a new service to production in under a day — securely and compliantly.”

item.title: FinOps for Cloud and Kubernetes
item.description:
Simple definition#

FinOps is an operational framework and cultural practice that maximises the business value of cloud (and now technology) spending through collaboration between engineering, finance and business — making cost visible, owned and optimised continuously.

item.title: Helm Charts
item.description:
Simple definition#

Helm is the package manager for Kubernetes. A chart is a versioned package of templated Kubernetes manifests; values customise it per environment; installing a chart creates a release that Helm can upgrade and roll back.

item.title: Service Mesh: Istio, Linkerd, Cilium and Ambient Mode
item.description:
Simple definition#

A service mesh is an infrastructure layer that handles service-to-service communication for you: encrypts it with mutual TLS, applies traffic rules (retries, timeouts, canary weights), enforces identity-based authorisation, and emits telemetry — without changing application code.

item.title: System Design: A Highly Available Multi-Region Kubernetes Platform
item.description:
The design brief#

“A digital bank’s customer-facing services (login, accounts, payments) must stay available 24x7 even if an entire cloud region fails. Design the Kubernetes platform and the failover approach.”

1. Requirements and SLOs#

Service tier SLO (availability) RTO RPO
Tier 0: login, balances, payments initiation 99.95% monthly ≤ 15 min regional failover ≤ 1 min (payments ledger: 0 for committed transactions)
Tier 1: statements, notifications 99.9% ≤ 1 h ≤ 15 min
Tier 2: analytics, back-office 99.5% ≤ 24 h ≤ 24 h

Other requirements: EU data residency (two EU regions), PCI DSS scope isolation, peak 3,000 requests/s, deployments several times a day without downtime.

item.title: CI/CD Pipelines and Progressive Delivery
item.description:
Simple definition#

  • Continuous integration (CI) — every change is merged often, built and tested automatically, producing a versioned artifact.
  • Continuous delivery (CD) — every artifact that passes the pipeline can be released at any time with the push of a button.
  • Continuous deployment — every passing change is released automatically.
  • Progressive delivery — releases are exposed gradually (canary, feature flags) and rolled back automatically if metrics degrade.

The pipeline#

Principles#

  1. Build once, promote the same artifact (by digest) through every environment; only configuration changes.
  2. Fast feedback: commit stage under 10 minutes; slower tests later and in parallel.
  3. Everything as code: pipelines, infrastructure, policies, environments.
  4. Shift security left but also verify at deploy time and runtime.
  5. Small batches: trunk-based development, short-lived branches, feature flags.
  6. CI pushes artifacts; CD pulls desired state — CI should not hold production cluster credentials (GitOps).

CI tools#

Tool Strengths Notes
GitHub Actions Huge marketplace, close to code, OIDC to clouds Self-hosted runners on Kubernetes (Actions Runner Controller)
GitLab CI Integrated DevSecOps platform, built-in scanners Strong for all-in-one setups
Jenkins Extremely flexible, huge plugin ecosystem Operational burden; plugin sprawl
Tekton Kubernetes-native CRDs (Tasks, Pipelines); OpenShift Pipelines Building block for platforms
Azure DevOps, CircleCI, Buildkite Managed options —

DevSecOps in the pipeline#

Stage Checks Tools (examples)
Code SAST, secrets detection, licence checks SonarQube, Semgrep, CodeQL, gitleaks
Dependencies SCA / vulnerable libraries Dependabot, Renovate, Snyk, OWASP Dependency-Check
IaC & manifests Misconfigurations, policies Checkov, Trivy config, Kyverno CLI, Conftest
Image CVEs, SBOM, provenance, signature Trivy, Grype, Syft, cosign, SLSA generators
Running app DAST OWASP ZAP
Runtime Behaviour detection Falco, cloud security tools

Deployment strategies#

Strategy Pros Cons
Rolling (Deployment default) Simple, no extra capacity Mixed versions during rollout; slow rollback
Blue-green Instant switch and rollback Double capacity; database changes must be compatible
Canary Real-traffic validation with small blast radius Needs good metrics and traffic splitting
Feature flags Decouple deploy from release; per-user targeting Flag debt; needs governance (OpenFeature standard)
Shadow / mirroring Test with production traffic, no user impact Side effects must be handled

Argo Rollouts and Flagger automate canary and blue-green on Kubernetes: shift traffic via Gateway API, mesh or ingress, run analysis against Prometheus/Datadog metrics (error rate, latency) and roll back automatically.

item.title: Kubernetes Security: From Supply Chain to Runtime
item.description:
Simple definition#

Kubernetes security is defence in depth across four layers — the 4Cs: Cloud (accounts, networks), Cluster (API access, policies), Container (images, runtime settings) and Code (dependencies, secrets). A weakness in an outer layer undermines everything inside it.

item.title: GitOps with Argo CD and Flux
item.description:
Simple definition#

GitOps manages infrastructure and applications by keeping their desired state in Git and running agents in the cluster that continuously pull that state and reconcile the cluster to match it. Git becomes the audit log, the review process and the rollback mechanism.

item.title: Release Orchestration with Digital.ai Release and Deploy
item.description:
Simple definition#

Release orchestration coordinates everything that has to happen for a release across many teams, tools and environments: builds, deployments, tests, security checks, approvals, change tickets, communications and evidence for auditors. CI/CD and GitOps automate a pipeline; release orchestration automates the release process around many pipelines.

item.title: About this handbook
item.description:
Purpose#

The Cloud Native & Platform Engineering Knowledge Hub explains how modern platforms are built and run — simply, with diagrams and flows — for architects, platform engineers, SREs and developers. It is the companion to the Java & Software Architecture Knowledge Hub and the Enterprise AI & Agentic AI Knowledge Hub.

item.title: Glossary
item.description:
Definitions are deliberately short. Follow the links for the full explanation.

A–C#

Admission control
Checks that validate or mutate API objects before they are stored. See Kubernetes security.
Argo CD
A GitOps controller that syncs Kubernetes clusters with Git. See GitOps.
Argo Rollouts
Progressive delivery controller for canary and blue-green rollouts. See CI/CD.
Backstage
An open-source developer portal framework (catalog, templates, docs, plugins). See IDPs.
Blue-green deployment
Switching all traffic between two complete environments. See CI/CD.
Burn rate
How fast an error budget is being consumed relative to the SLO. See SRE.
Canary release
Gradually shifting traffic to a new version while analysing metrics. See CI/CD.
cgroups
Linux control groups that limit a process’s resources. See Containers.
CNI / CRI / CSI
Standard interfaces for networking, container runtimes and storage. See Architecture.
Crossplane
A Kubernetes-based control plane for provisioning infrastructure through APIs. See IDPs.
Custom resource / operator
A new API type and the controller that automates it. See Architecture.

D–G#

Developer experience (DevEx)
How developers perceive their work environment: feedback loops, cognitive load, flow. See DevEx.
Digital.ai Release / Deploy
Enterprise release orchestration and model-driven deployment tools. See Release orchestration.
DORA metrics
Deployment frequency, lead time, change failure rate, recovery time. See CI/CD.
Dynamic Resource Allocation (DRA)
Kubernetes API for requesting GPUs and other devices. See Workloads.
eBPF
Programs running safely in the Linux kernel, used for networking, security and observability. See Networking.
Error budget
The allowed unreliability, 1 − SLO. See SRE.
etcd
The distributed key-value store holding Kubernetes state. See Architecture.
FinOps
Practice of managing cloud value through engineering–finance collaboration. See FinOps.
FOCUS
FinOps Open Cost and Usage Specification for billing data. See FinOps.
Gateway API
The successor to Ingress for routing traffic into and within clusters. See Networking.
GitOps
Declarative desired state in Git, pulled and reconciled by agents. See GitOps.
Golden path
An opinionated, supported way to perform a common task. See Platform engineering.

H–O#

Helm
The Kubernetes package manager (charts, values, releases). See Helm.
HPA / VPA / KEDA
Autoscalers for replicas, requests and event-driven scaling. See Workloads.
Internal developer platform (IDP)
Integrated tools, APIs and golden paths for self-service delivery. See IDPs.
Karpenter
A node autoscaler that provisions right-sized nodes and consolidates. See Workloads.
Kyverno
A Kubernetes-native policy engine. See Security.
NetworkPolicy
Rules restricting Pod traffic. See Networking.
Observability
Ability to understand system behaviour from telemetry. See Observability.
OpenShift
Red Hat’s enterprise Kubernetes platform. See OpenShift.
OpenTelemetry (OTel)
The vendor-neutral standard for telemetry. See Observability.

P–Z#

PodDisruptionBudget (PDB)
Limits voluntary disruptions to an application. See Resilience.
Pod Security Standards
Privileged, baseline and restricted security profiles. See Security.
RBAC
Role-based access control for the Kubernetes API. See Security.
RPO / RTO
Maximum acceptable data loss and downtime. See Resilience.
SBOM
Software bill of materials. See Security.
Service mesh
Infrastructure layer for mTLS, traffic control and telemetry. See Service mesh.
SLI / SLO / SLA
Indicator, objective and agreement for reliability. See SRE.
SLSA
Supply-chain Levels for Software Artifacts — build provenance framework. See Security.
Team Topologies
Model of team types and interactions. See Platform engineering.
Toil
Manual, repetitive, automatable operational work. See SRE.
